text:
Chapter Eight


Maggie’s arm was fine. Sure, she hadn’t slept in days, because the skin was aching and tight across her forearm. The ghoul’s handprint was seared into her skin, but the nurse in the infirmary promised it would disappear in a few days as the wound healed. She had given her a medicated cream, and it was helping, but the handprint was red and raw. Still, if you asked Maggie, she was just fine.


Dean Clearwater had already given her an earful on Monday morning about putting herself in danger. He had been waiting at her office, actually pacing in front of the door with nervous energy.


“Why didn’t you call a wardsmith?” he demanded instead of starting with hello or good morning. It was nice, actually, to have someone be so worried about her. She hadn’t bothered to tell her parents about her run-in with the ghoul during their weekly phone call, concerned she would worry them or, worse, that they wouldn’t care at all.


“We did,” she explained. “But Rodrigo already had one ghoul attack last week, and the wardsmith didn’t bother to banish it. They just put up some shoddy ward that clearly didn’t work.”


Dean Clearwater sighed. “You and Dr. Hawberry are very talented, but you put yourselves in unnecessary danger. After a night out, I presume?”


Maggie’s face flushed. That wasn’t really his business. She bit her lip, thinking of the dean’s warnings about keeping Taliesin happy, about the precarious position she suddenly found herself in at Hawthorn. She didn’t want to anger the dean more, but after Friday night, she couldn’t quite stop herself from asking, “Clearly this pall is dangerous. That ghoul never would have been in Rodrigo’s basement if it weren’t for the pall’s magic feeding it and wearing on his wards. Why hasn’t the pall been dissipated yet?”


The dean rubbed one of his fluffy white eyebrows. “Dr. Taliesin has taken the lead on developing the dissipation spell, and he is working diligently on it.” Maggie crossed her arms, avoiding the aching burn, and raised her eyebrows. Dean Clearwater sighed.


She wanted to yell that Taliesin was putting an entire town in danger, but Maggie managed to keep her cool. “What about Galloway?”


“This incident has made it clear that we need to fortify wards beyond the campus boundary. I’ve already sent a notification out to the local wardsmith office, who will take care of the spellwork to strengthen the wards around town.” Maggie opened her mouth to say something, but Dean Clearwater interrupted her. “I’ll make sure it’s good work. Not the subpar warding done at the bar.”


It wasn’t enough, but it was something. After Maggie promised him she wouldn’t put herself in danger or allow Dahlia to confront any more ghouls, the dean seemed satisfied, giving her a small pat on the arm before returning to the admin building.


The rest of the week, Maggie went through the motions, avoiding Taliesin as much as she could. If he had heard about the ghoul in Rodrigo’s basement, he certainly hadn’t bothered to see if she was as fine as she claimed. The few times Maggie had seen him over the week he’d looked as drawn and weary as she felt. Even her students were subdued. She didn’t know if it was their approaching finals, the gloomy weather that had stuck around all week, or the effects of the pall seeping down through the floors, but there was none of the usual excitement that should have accompanied the end of a semester, buoyed by warm weather and sunny skies.


On Friday afternoon, after a particularly glum session of Advanced Translation, she was relieved when she returned to her office to find it empty. If Taliesin had been in their shared space that morning, there was no evidence of it.


Maggie turned on some music, kept the lights low, and began working on the spells she was preparing for her final exams. It wasn’t long before she was interrupted by a knock on her door. A student with a backpack slung over one shoulder stood waiting, looking around her and into the office. “Is Dr. T here?”


“He’s not. Did you have a meeting with him?”


“No, but these are his posted office hours.”


Maggie tried to keep her expression neutral, but a bubbling fury rose in her. Her arm ached, she was freezing, she hadn’t seen the sun in days, and she couldn’t focus for five minutes in her office without someone looking for him. And she couldn’t believe he would miss his own office hours. It was so inconsiderate to his students. “Hmm, well, I’m afraid he isn’t here. You can send him an email to schedule some time. Or”—she nearly stopped herself from saying it, but she did feel bad for the kid—“you’re welcome to wait for him here if you want.” She gestured to the couch, and the student followed her into the office. He gave her a nod of thanks and then sank into the cushions, putting in a pair of headphones. The faint beat of a song she recognized played, and he tapped his foot while he waited. After fifteen minutes, she gestured for him to take his headphones out.


“I’m so sorry. I’m sure something just came up.”


The student nodded. “Thanks. I hope everything is all right.”


Maggie frowned as he left. She hadn’t even considered the fact that anything might be wrong, and she felt a momentary wave of guilt wash over her.


The guilt vanished, though, after the second, third, and then fourth interruption, when students looking for Taliesin during his office hours knocked on the door. She finally took out a piece of paper and wrote in block letters:


DR. TALIESIN IS NOT HERE. IF YOU NEED HIM, EMAIL HIM.


When she couldn’t find her tape, she stuck it to the door with a quick bit of magic and, pleased with herself, got back to work.


If more students or other professors came by to find Taliesin, they didn’t bother her. The afternoon stretched on, and Maggie completed most of the exam prep work she had set out to finish, relieved to finally get something substantial done. As she packed up her work, filing it in folders she would carry to the exam, the door to her office opened.


She was about to announce that Taliesin was still out when she turned. It wasn’t a student or another professor in the doorway, but Taliesin himself.


He gripped the door frame as if he might collapse if he let it go. He sighed and heaved himself into the room, every step an effort, before he collapsed onto the sofa, the fainting couch nearly earning its name. The sign she’d attached to the door was crumpled in his hand.


She jumped to her feet. “Taliesin!” She had meant to yell at him, to hold on to her anger and give him a piece of her mind, but instead she was closing the small distance between them. There was a sheen of sweat on his brow, and he couldn’t catch his breath as he leaned forward, his head in his hands. “Please do not vomit in our office,” Maggie begged.


Taliesin didn’t respond right away, steadying himself against the nausea, but then managed to eke out a single word. “Ours?” he asked, peeking out from his hands. He immediately groaned and lowered his head back between his knees.


Maggie opened her bottom desk drawer and rummaged through it until she found what she was looking for. Ginger oil and ginger chews. She unwrapped the candy. “Here,” she said, and he managed to sit upright, taking the candy from her open palm and placing it between his lips.


“Thanks,” he muttered, sucking on the ginger chew with obvious relief. He leaned back, eyes closed, and took deep breaths. His skin was pale, with a sickly green pallor that was fading, and his breathing slowly became more natural. “I’m sorry for whatever caused you to put this up,” he said, holding the crumpled paper up for her to see.


“You missed your office hours.”


“Shit,” he swore, and she raised an eyebrow. She knew Taliesin couldn’t be professional all the time, but she didn’t think she’d heard him curse once. “Shit,” he repeated and made a move to stand up, but he immediately sat back down, swaying slightly.


“This is pall sickness,” she said gently, unwrapping another candy and holding it out to him. “How long were you up there today?”


He took the candy and stared at it a moment. “All day,” he finally said.


“All day?” she repeated, her voice surprisingly shrill. “No wonder you’re about to barf.”


“Please,” he said. “Do not say that word.”


“Upchuck?”


“Maggie.”


“Hurl?”


“Maggie,” he practically growled.


“Sorry,” she said, though she didn’t particularly feel it. Instead, she felt a surprising thrill at the way he’d said her name. “Look, this has gone on long enough. You know how dangerous it is to stay within a pall. What are you doing up there?”


He shook his head, jaw clenched. His tone was cold when he spoke again. “We don’t need to change the status quo now, Dr. Linden. You keep to your work, and I’ll keep to mine.”


She leaned against her desk and crossed her arms. She wore an oversized sweater with bell sleeves, anything to keep the fabric from touching the ghoul burn on her arm. Taliesin looked up at her from the couch, and his expression held something she couldn’t name, but it felt like a dare. “Who is helping you develop the counterspell?”


“No one. And I want it that way.”


She threw her hands up, feeling the skin pull at the edges of the burn. “What kind of masochistic…You know, if you were as good as you think you are, that pall wouldn’t have been cast in the first place.”


He laughed bitterly, shaking his head. “Believe me, that is not the problem. I know exactly how good I am.”


“Then what is the problem?” Maggie wasn’t used to yelling at colleagues, let alone someone as important as Taliesin, but she was so angry, and he was being so foolishly prideful. “You practically shoved me down the stairs when you were warding the building against the pall that day. You don’t think I’m good enough to keep up with you? Don’t think there are a dozen professors here who can do the same work as you?”


He couldn’t even look at her as he said, “Quite the contrary, actually.”


“Then what?”


He sat up, leaning forward on his knees until the two of them were mere inches apart. She smelled the sulfur clinging to his clothes first, but then that familiar smell of his cologne beneath it and the spice of the ginger chew. When he didn’t answer, Maggie kept talking. “You seem fine with inconveniencing an entire academic building,” she went on. And then, thinking of what the dean had told her earlier that week, “And there’s no way Dean Clearwater is okay with this scheme of yours with graduation coming up and all the donors that are going to be on campus.”


Taliesin scoffed. “It’s always about the budget! If I had known how much of my time at Hawthorn was going to be spent pinching pennies, I would have stayed at Dartwood.”


“You would have been doing us all a favor, then!” Maggie’s face burned as she shouted it, and her voice carried an embarrassing screech, but she couldn’t believe he dared to bring up the budget. Not to her. Not now.


To his credit, Taliesin looked ashamed. Or wounded. She couldn’t quite read his expression as he scrunched up his face and made a sound somewhere between a groan and a sigh. He leaned back against the couch, and they both found something, anything else to stare at in the office, unwilling to look at each other after their outbursts. Maggie stared at a particularly worn part of the emerald couch, threadbare and showing some of the stuffing.


Maggie was the first to break the painful, awkward silence. “Why won’t you let anyone help you?”


His voice had the steady beat of a recitation. “Pall sickness develops after prolonged exposure to the vaporized ectoplasm that feeds a pall. After light to moderate exposure, small particles, constructed primarily of elements found only in realms unseen, can cause fatigue, nausea, vomiting, headache, melancholia, and confusion. Prolonged exposure can cause more serious effects, such as a temporary loss of consciousness and, in extreme cases, death. Frequent short-term exposure is associated with shortened lifespans due to all causes.”


Maggie rolled her eyes. He was so godsdamn annoying. “Thank you for reciting the textbook definition of pall sickness, but I already knew all that.”


“Then what aren’t you getting? I’m not risking anyone else,” he snapped, looking up at her. His tone wasn’t angry, not the way Maggie’s had been, but it had a sharpness to it. “Not their safety or their sanity. My students were terrified that day because of a stupid mistake that I made. I’m not going to let anyone else suffer the consequences of my mistake. Least of all you.”


“I’m already suffering!” Maggie slid her sleeve up to her elbow, revealing the ghoul’s blistering and raw handprint. Taliesin stood with a sharp intake of breath, but there was so little space between her desk and the couch that he towered over her. He stared at the wound, and then his fingers were on her, so gentle, turning her arm so he could look at the burn. She was confused by the graze of his touch, by his concern, by the goose bumps she watched rise on her skin.


He finally looked up from her arm, a question in his expression. She swallowed. “There was a ghoul. At Rodrigo’s downtown. It’s my friend’s dive—”


“I know Rodrigo’s,” he interrupted, and she bit her cheek to keep from snapping at him.


“He’d already called a wardsmith, and they did a shoddy job getting rid of it, so Dahlia…Dr. Hawberry and I went to the basement to eradicate it. It was fine, honestly. It barely got to us before we finished the banishment spell. It was just bad luck that it grabbed my arm.”


“A banishment spell takes at least eight minutes,” he said, his voice tight.


“I’m aware.”


“And even longer to properly draw a rune.”


“Dahlia is the best. She did it in four,” Maggie said, and she meant it to lighten the mood, but Taliesin’s expression was still pained. He cradled her arm, looking at the wound as if he could find a new way to heal it that the nurse hadn’t thought of yet. “It…it’s fine. It doesn’t hurt much.”


She gently tugged her arm from his grip, and he seemed reluctant to let her go. When he finally did and she drew her sleeve back down over the burn, she could still feel the places his fingers had touched, as sharp as the ghoul’s.


“Dean Clearwater thinks I have help. And I do—colleagues from Dartwood are working on the problem remotely, with samples I’ve sent them.” He paused. “But Dean Clearwater doesn’t know I’ve been going into the pall alone, or that I haven’t technically put together a team to dissipate it.”


Maggie raised an eyebrow at that news. “And how long do you think you can coast on being Arthur fucking Taliesin before he starts wondering why his third floor is still attracting every ghost, ghoul, and banshee for a hundred miles?”


“I don’t know,” he admitted with a sigh.


An idea began to take root, and before she could doubt herself too much, she blurted, “You need help.” He looked up at her with something like indignation. “No, you need my help.” She marveled at the words even as they came out of her mouth. The last thing she wanted to do this summer was help Taliesin do the spellwork necessary to get rid of the pall. Tedious calculations, rare ingredients they’d have to hunt down, extra translations, but if he was going to be this stubborn…at least she already knew about his problem.


“What exactly are you proposing?” he asked her, eyebrows arched until they disappeared behind his hair.


He was still so close to her, and it was overwhelming, so she returned to her desk chair, her shoulder brushing his chest as she walked past. She felt better, though, with even that small amount of distance between them. He stared at the spot where she had been standing until she rummaged through her drawer for another ginger candy, placing it on the desk. He grabbed it and she marveled at the way she felt strangely attuned to every one of his movements.


She took a deep breath. “I’ll put aside my summer schedule and help you. Between the two of us, we should be able to figure out why you can’t get rid of this pall. Together, we can have it clear by the end of June.”


It looked like gears were moving in his head, as if he was trying to determine her intentions. “If I refuse your help?”


“I’m not going to tell Dean Clearwater, if that’s what you’re afraid of. That’s your own mess. But you can’t stop me from researching it on my own.” She paused for a moment, thinking about the way his fingers felt on her skin, about how he seemed so afraid of anyone else being exposed to the pall. She shrugged dramatically. “I can access the third floor as easily as you can. I don’t mind working by myself.”


He stared at Maggie and asked, “What do you want?”


“I want my office back, Taliesin.”


For the first time since he had collapsed on the couch, his expression lightened, his lips curving into a grin. “I thought it was ours.” Her stomach gave a traitorous flip, and she wondered if he could see it on her face. He unwrapped the ginger candy that was still in his palm and placed it on his tongue.


“What else?” he asked.


She didn’t hesitate. “Eight thousand dollars from next year’s alchemy budget, returned to the linguistics department for special projects,” she said with a nervous swallow.


She waited for him to push back and say she couldn’t risk her life. She wanted him to say it was too much money. Waited for him to question why she had asked for eight thousand dollars exactly so she could stay mad at him and start yelling. Any of that would be better than whatever this strange, agonizing tension was between them. Instead, he kept looking at her with that grin that seemed to say he was getting exactly what he wanted somehow.


Finally, it was as if his mind had caught up with what she was saying. “Returned?” he asked, a small frown on his face, as if he didn’t know exactly what he’d done during that budget meeting in November.


“Yes, returned,” she repeated. “That’s the least you could do.”


After another agonizing moment when she waited for him to ask for an explanation, he instead said, “Fine. I can agree to your terms.”


So, before she could think too hard about it, she held out her hand for him to shake. He stared at it for a second and then reached for her.


Why did it feel, suddenly, like she was the one who had bargained something away? She didn’t have time to think about it before his hand was enveloping hers, and she had that strange sensation of smallness again as his fingers closed around her palm, their calloused pads reaching down to the soft skin at her wrist.
